## Before the bench {.center}

### What you are about to measure

A ratiometric Hall sensor reports a field relative to its own supply, and a
small magnet's field is a strongly nonlinear function of distance.

By the end of the session you will know:

- what "ratiometric" buys you, quantified against a drifting supply, not
  just asserted;
- how to fit that nonlinear curve explicitly, and use it to choose a working
  range from two competing criteria, not a guess;
- how the same sensor, on the beam, gives a second and independent estimate
  of the beam's stiffness — checked against
  [M1's](../M1-strain-load/index.qmd) strain-based one.

### The rule of the session

::: {.callout-important}
## A working range is a choice, with a criterion

"Close to the magnet" is not a design. Every working point in this session
is chosen against two curves — resolution and curvature — plotted together,
not picked because it looked reasonable.
:::

## At the bench {.center}

### What you will build

A micrometer stage carrying a small magnet, a fixed Hall sensor with its
supply logged on a second channel, and — for the cross-check — the same
sensor mounted at the beam tip.

::: {.smaller}
| Run(s) | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Calibration sweep, 12 distances | The nonlinear $V(d)$ curve |
| Supply-drift, displacement fixed | Ratiometric vs. absolute reading |
| Cross-check masses (same as M1) | Tip displacement under known loads |
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## What ruins the session

Recording the **intended** micrometer step instead of its **actual**
reading loses the backlash the fit needs to see. Bumping the stage during
the supply-drift run confounds the one effect that run exists to isolate.
:::

### Then

Open [the handbook](handbook.qmd) for the full procedure, and one of the two
analysis templates — [Python](analysis-py.qmd) or [R](analysis-r.qmd).

They have the same sections and produce the same numbers. Both ship with
reference data, so you can read the whole analysis before you wire anything.

## What you should come away with {.center}

### Three sentences you should be able to defend

1. "Our calibration curve gave $A = \dots$, $d_0 = \dots$ mm (fixed
   $n = 3$), with a residual of $\dots$ mm across the sweep."
2. "We chose a working point at $d = \dots$ mm, where the resolution was
   $\dots$ mm and the linearization error over our excursion was
   $\dots$ mm — both inside our stated tolerance."
3. "A $\dots\,\%$ supply drift produced $\dots$ mm of apparent displacement
   read absolute, and $\dots$ mm read ratiometric."

If you can say those three — and, having also run M1, a fourth about
$E_\mathrm{M1}/E_\mathrm{M2}$ — with your own numbers in them, the session
worked.
